items.followUp: A car accelerates uniformly from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. Use the second equation of motion to find its displacement.

rubric.why: Credit for using the speed–time graph to represent displacement.
rubric.description: Identifies the area under the speed–time graph as displacement.
rubric.how: State that displacement is the area under the graph.

rubric.why: The graph area must be expressed using the initial speed, final speed and time.
rubric.description: Writes the trapezium area relation and uses v = u + at.
rubric.how: Show s = ½(u + v)t and substitute v = u + at.

rubric.why: Credit for correctly simplifying the substitution.
rubric.description: Obtains the second equation of motion.
rubric.how: Simplify to s = ut + ½at².

rubric.why: The derived result must be clearly identified as the required equation.
rubric.description: States the final equation as the second equation of motion.
rubric.how: Write the result clearly as the second equation of motion.

modelAnswer: For uniform acceleration, displacement s is the area under the speed–time graph.
The graph forms a trapezium, so s = ½(u + v)t.
From the first equation of motion, v = u + at.
Substituting, s = ½(u + u + at)t.
Therefore, s = ut + ½at², the second equation of motion.

items.followUp: Define potential energy and derive the expression for the gravitational potential energy of an object raised through height h.

rubric.why: The definition must connect kinetic energy with an object's motion.
rubric.description: Defines kinetic energy as energy possessed due to motion.
rubric.how: State that kinetic energy is the energy an object possesses because of its motion.

rubric.why: The derivation begins by equating the work done to the gain in kinetic energy.
rubric.description: Uses work done W = Fs and Newton's second law F = ma.
rubric.how: Write W = Fs and F = ma.

rubric.why: This motion relation connects the work done with the change in speed.
rubric.description: Uses the equation v² − u² = 2as to obtain W = ½m(v² − u²).
rubric.how: Substitute F = ma and as = (v² − u²)/2 into W = Fs.

rubric.why: For an object starting from rest, the final result is the standard kinetic-energy equation.
rubric.description: Sets u = 0 and obtains the kinetic-energy equation.
rubric.how: For u = 0, write KE = ½mv².

modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by an object due to its motion.
The work done to give an object speed v from rest is W = Fs.
Using F = ma and v² − u² = 2as, W = mas = ½m(v² − u²).
For an object starting from rest, u = 0; therefore, KE = W = ½mv².

items.followUp: A steering wheel has a radius of 20 cm. Equal and opposite forces of 12 N act tangentially on opposite sides. Find the torque of the couple.

rubric.why: The stated radius must be converted correctly to SI units.
rubric.description: Converts the steering-wheel radius to 0.16 m.
rubric.how: Convert 16 cm to 0.16 m.

rubric.why: For opposite tangential forces, the perpendicular separation is the wheel's diameter.
rubric.description: Finds the couple arm as the diameter, 2r = 0.32 m.
rubric.how: Calculate the perpendicular distance between the forces as 2 × 0.16 m.

rubric.why: Torque of a couple is force multiplied by the perpendicular distance between the forces.
rubric.description: States the torque-of-a-couple relation.
rubric.how: Write torque = one force × perpendicular distance between the forces.

rubric.why: Substitution gives the torque in terms of the force, since no force magnitude is provided.
rubric.description: Substitutes the couple arm to obtain τ = 0.32F N·m.
rubric.how: Write τ = F × 0.32 m = 0.32F N·m.

rubric.why: A numerical torque cannot be obtained without the magnitude of either force.
rubric.description: Notes that the question lacks the force magnitude, so no numerical torque can be calculated.
rubric.how: State that the torque remains 0.32F N·m and that a force value is needed for a numerical answer.

modelAnswer: Given radius r = 16 cm = 0.16 m.
For two equal and opposite tangential forces, the couple arm is the diameter: d = 2r = 0.32 m.
Torque of a couple, τ = Fd.
Therefore, τ = F × 0.32 m = 0.32F N·m, where F is the magnitude of either force.
The force magnitude is not given, so a numerical value for the torque cannot be found.

items.followUp: Derive the expression for pressure at depth h in a liquid, and state what happens to pressure if the depth is doubled.

rubric.why: Pressure is defined as normal force per unit area.
rubric.description: Starts with the definition of pressure.
rubric.how: Write P = F/A.

rubric.why: The force exerted by the liquid column is its weight.
rubric.description: Identifies the liquid's force as its weight.
rubric.how: Write F = mg.

rubric.why: The liquid-column mass must be expressed using its density and volume.
rubric.description: Uses m = ρV and V = Ah.
rubric.how: For a column of area A and depth h, write m = ρAh.

rubric.why: Substitution yields the required liquid-pressure formula.
rubric.description: Derives P = ρgh.
rubric.how: Substitute F = mg = ρAhg into P = F/A and simplify.

modelAnswer: Pressure is force per unit area: P = F/A.
For a liquid column of depth h and cross-sectional area A, its volume is V = Ah.
Its mass is m = ρV = ρAh, so its weight is F = mg = ρAhg.
Therefore, P = F/A = ρAhg/A = ρgh.

items.followUp: Estimate the number of seconds in one week, showing the conversion from days to seconds.

rubric.why: Credit for converting one day from hours to seconds.
rubric.description: Uses 24 hours, 60 minutes per hour and 60 seconds per minute.
rubric.how: Calculate 1 day = 24 × 60 × 60 s.

rubric.why: The answer should give the seconds in a day and a suitable estimate.
rubric.description: Gives 86,400 s, approximately 10⁵ s.
rubric.how: State 1 day = 86,400 s ≈ 10⁵ s.

modelAnswer: 1 day = 24 h × 60 min/h × 60 s/min.
1 day = 86,400 s ≈ 8.64 × 10⁴ s, or approximately 10⁵ s.

items.followUp: From the list kilogram, joule, second, kelvin and coulomb, identify the SI base units.

rubric.why: Metre, ampere and mole are SI base units among the listed options.
rubric.description: Identifies at least one correct base unit.
rubric.how: Select metre, ampere and/or mole.

rubric.why: Full credit requires identifying all base units and excluding derived units.
rubric.description: Identifies all three base units and distinguishes watt and newton as derived units.
rubric.how: State that metre, ampere and mole are base units; watt and newton are derived units.

modelAnswer: The SI base units in the list are metre, ampere and mole.
Watt and newton are derived units.

items.followUp: Define uniform circular motion and give one example.

rubric.why: The definition must specify that the path is circular.
rubric.description: States that the object moves along a circular path.
rubric.how: Include the phrase circular path or equivalent.

rubric.why: Circular motion is described relative to a centre or fixed axis.
rubric.description: States that the motion is around a fixed centre or axis.
rubric.how: Mention the fixed centre or axis about which the object moves.

modelAnswer: Circular motion is the motion of an object along a circular path about a fixed point or axis.

items.followUp: A 3 kg object moves at 4 m/s. Calculate its momentum and state its direction.

rubric.why: Momentum is defined as the product of mass and velocity.
rubric.description: Defines momentum in terms of mass and velocity.
rubric.how: State that momentum equals mass multiplied by velocity.

rubric.why: The standard equation and vector nature complete the definition.
rubric.description: Gives p = mv and identifies momentum as a vector quantity.
rubric.how: Write p = mv and note that momentum has the direction of velocity.

modelAnswer: Momentum is the product of an object's mass and velocity.
It is given by p = mv and is a vector quantity, in the direction of the velocity.
